title: IAsyncEnumerable and await foreach (streaming async sequences)
hook: IEnumerable cannot await between items. IAsyncEnumerable is the language's way to pull the next page of queue messages or CSV chunks without buffering the whole stream in memory.

blocks.text: IAsyncEnumerable<T> (introduced in C# 8) is an asynchronous sequence you consume with await foreach. The producer method is async IAsyncEnumerable<T> and uses yield return between awaits. Between yields you can await I/O — fetching the next page of results, reading the next file chunk, or receiving the next batch of queue messages. The compiler generates a state machine implementing IAsyncEnumerator<T>. DisposeAsync runs when the foreach exits, including on break and exceptions.

entries.plainDefinition: An asynchronous sequence that produces items over time, with awaits between them.
Consumer syntax for IAsyncEnumerable. Awaits each MoveNextAsync before accessing Current.
entries.example: await foreach (var msg in stream) { await HandleAsync(msg); }

entries.plainDefinition: An attribute on the CancellationToken parameter so await foreach can pass its token into the iterator.
Extension that attaches a CancellationToken to an IAsyncEnumerable for await foreach.

blocks.text: Buffering an entire CSV import or SQS drain into a List allocates memory proportional to the total size. IAsyncEnumerable lets you process one page at a time — constant memory regardless of total volume. If the next step needs the full dataset for a sort, streaming buys nothing. For pull-based pipelines where the consumer controls pace, IAsyncEnumerable is the right abstraction.

blocks.title: Cancellation wiring
blocks.body: Use [EnumeratorCancellation] on the iterator's token parameter. Without it, WithCancellation from the consumer side is ignored — a common bug during host shutdown.

diagram.title: IAsyncEnumerable pull stream
diagram.source:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Consumer await foreach
  participant I as IAsyncEnumerable iterator
  participant N as Network
  C->>I: MoveNextAsync
  I->>N: await fetch page
  N-->>I: data
  I-->>C: true + Current item
  C->>C: process item
  C->>I: MoveNextAsync
  I-->>C: false — done
  C->>I: DisposeAsync

snippet.label: Paging SQS with await foreach
snippet.explanation: Each page is awaited. Callers see a stream of messages, not a List allocated for the whole drain. EnumeratorCancellation wires the consumer's token into the iterator.

snippet.label: Streaming CSV lines without loading the file
snippet.explanation: One row at a time, one await per line. Memory stays constant regardless of file size.

snippet.label: When streaming does not help
snippet.explanation: If the next step needs all data for a sort or aggregate, IAsyncEnumerable buys nothing. Choose the right tool for the access pattern.

snippet.label: Backpressure with IAsyncEnumerable vs Channel
snippet.explanation: IAsyncEnumerable naturally backpressures via pull. Channels add an explicit bounded buffer when producer and consumer run independently.

blocks.title: Async iteration in C# vs JavaScript
Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Forgetting [EnumeratorCancellation] so WithCancellation is ignored. Calling ToListAsync() on a huge import and recreating the memory problem. Yielding after disposing the resource the next MoveNextAsync still needs. Mixing yield return with side effects you cannot undo unless the consumer contract is clear.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: compare memory working set of ToListAsync versus await foreach on a 10 GB CSV import — streaming stays flat, buffering spikes linearly. IAsyncEnumerable uses a compiler-generated async iterator state machine (like async methods but with MoveNextAsync). ConfigureAwait flows through await foreach automatically. For backpressure, the consumer controls pace — if HandleAsync is slow, the producer naturally waits at the next MoveNextAsync.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Using IAsyncEnumerable then calling ToListAsync immediately — defeats the purpose. Forgetting [EnumeratorCancellation] and wondering why host shutdown does not stop the iterator. Saying await foreach runs the producer on a new thread — it is pull-based on the consumer's thread. Choosing IAsyncEnumerable when you need the full sorted dataset anyway.

interviewTakeaways: IAsyncEnumerable is a pull-based async stream — await foreach calls MoveNextAsync, which awaits I/O between items.
Use [EnumeratorCancellation] so WithCancellation from the consumer wires into the iterator's token parameter.
In production, compare working set: streaming stays flat on large imports; ToListAsync spikes memory linearly.

60s: IAsyncEnumerable streams pages with await between yields. await foreach pulls one item at a time. EnumeratorCancellation wires cancellation. ToListAsync defeats streaming. Use Channels for push backpressure.
Follow-up: when would Channel<T> be better than IAsyncEnumerable?
commonPitfalls: Calling ToListAsync on a huge stream gets you rejected — you recreated the memory problem you were solving.
Forgetting [EnumeratorCancellation] — WithCancellation is silently ignored and shutdown does not stop the iterator.
Strong answer: 'IAsyncEnumerable for pull-based paging with constant memory. Channels when producer outpaces consumer and I need bounded backpressure.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS async generators (async function*) plus for await...of are the same pull-stream idea. C# yield return in async IAsyncEnumerable is the closest language twin.
TypeScript types async iterators with AsyncIterable<T> and AsyncIterator<T>. C# IAsyncEnumerable<T> is the BCL interface with built-in LINQ support via System.Linq.Async.
